title: Machine judging: Accuracy cannot establish legitimate authority
desc: Separates capacity and impartiality claims from consent, challenge rights, legal development and public confidence.

kps.k: The central dispute concerns delegating judicial authority, not simply introducing AI into courts.
kps.d: The sources distinguish administrative automation, assistance to accountable professionals, direct guidance to unrepresented people and autonomous adjudication. Canadian Judicial Council guidance categorically prohibits delegating judicial decisions, regardless of a program’s capabilities; England and Wales guidance permits secondary assistance but requires judges to read underlying documents. By contrast, Vos’s 2026 lectures predict machine determination of some routine disputes, driven by anticipated reliability, speed and cost. His June remarks acknowledge that specialist systems still need development and testing. These positions differ in institutional purpose and time horizon: current restrictions do not establish permanent technical impossibility, and forecasts do not establish present authority to automate.

qs.q: It must be unequivocally understood that no judge is permitted to delegate decision-making authority, whether to a law clerk, administrative assistant, or computer program, regardless of their capabilities.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Canadian Courts (Canadian Judicial Council, First Edition, September 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: AI tools may assist, but they cannot replace direct judicial engagement with evidence.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence (AI) — Guidance for Judicial Office Holders (refreshed 31 October 2025) · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Capacity and access arguments support experimentation, but faster production need not produce faster justice.
kps.d: Roberts identifies practical assistance with court forms; Vos advocates integrated online information, advice and resolution rather than merely digitising lengthy proceedings. McCormack envisages automated dispute resolution reaching previously uneconomic micro-claims. The E46 podcast speaker cites 2,500 annual cases per state trial judge to motivate added capacity, without demonstrating AI’s effect on backlogs. Counterarguments identify increased demand and processing burdens: judicial interviewees and survey respondents fear voluminous motions, additional authorities and prolonged weak cases. These comments offer plausible mechanisms and experiential testimony, not measured net effects on court throughput.

qs.q: It drives new, highly accessible tools that provide answers to basic questions, including where to find templates and court forms, how to fill them out, and where to bring them for presentation to the judge—all without leaving home.
qs.a: 2023 Year-End Report on the Federal Judiciary · Regulators & courts · 2023

qs.q: The idea is that any citizen with a legal problem can go online and be directed to the trusted legal information or advice and the trusted dispute resolution service that they need to resolve their particular kind of dispute.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence and the Judiciary — Sir Geoffrey Vos MR, lecture to the Judicial Institute for Scotland (Edinburgh, 30 April 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Technical accuracy does not settle adjudicative legitimacy or control over legal development.
kps.d: Is Law Computable? challenges the inference from convincing outputs or successful prediction to legitimate judgment: adjudication involves contestable interpretation, deliberation and institutional authority. Roberts’s 2023 report reserves contextual appellate judgment and legal development for humans; the ABA Year 1 excerpt republishes that position rather than independently establishing it. A View of How Language Models Will Transform Law argues that even accurate AI could pursue unwanted social goals if allowed to make law autonomously. Artificial Wisdom? offers a narrower, expressly conditional philosophical limit based on subjective experience and moral judgment, not an empirical proof that machines cannot judge.

qs.q: In the context of legal decision making, judgment is not a purely predictive process; it is the out- come of deliberation and contestation.
qs.a: Is Law Computable? From Rule of Law to Legal Singularity (introductory chapter to Is Law Computable? Critical Perspectives on Law and Artificial Intelligence) · Academia · 2020

qs.q: AI is based largely on existing information, which can inform but not make such decisions.
qs.a: 2023 Year-End Report on the Federal Judiciary · Regulators & courts · 2023

kps.k: Claims of machine impartiality face competing accounts of both human and algorithmic bias.
kps.d: McCormack treats differing human priors and open-ended legal standards as sources of subjectivity; the essay discussed in her podcast proposes potentially fairer assistance, not literal replacement of judges. Other sources warn that training data, design choices and prompts embed values rather than eliminate them. Surden illustrates how prompt wording can shift interpretive emphasis. Ethics of AI in Law makes comparative accuracy an empirical question and cautions against comparing imperfect machines with idealised humans: human reasoning also resists direct inspection. The supplied material does not establish general superiority in fairness for either decision-maker.

qs.q: So it always felt to me that bias—in the way that we all have bias, just human bias, inherent bias—is part of judicial decision-making.
qs.a: What Role Will AI Play in Transforming Justice Systems? — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: We are here today to have a conversation about these topics to ensure that lawyers understand that when they ask legal questions of these AI systems, these value and interpretive choices are often implicitly occurring in the background in a non-transparent manner.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence and Law—An Overview of Recent Technological Changes: Keynote Address at the 2024 Ira C. Rothgerber Jr. & Silicon Flatirons Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Constitutional Law · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Consent, rights of challenge and public confidence distinguish machine arbitration from imposed court adjudication.
kps.d: Vos supports parties choosing final machine determination in arbitration while requiring informed consent and legislative debate before replacing human court adjudication. He leaves Article 6 compatibility and a universal final human appeal unresolved. The European Ethical Charter conditions contemplated online pre-litigation resolution on later access to a judge; UNESCO requires meaningful understanding and challenge of AI-assisted detention decisions. Separately, Vos, Roberts and judicial interviewees distinguish acceptable outcomes from feeling heard and trusting the process. Roberts’s cited fairness studies concern public perceptions, not comparative substantive fairness.

qs.q: In a democratic society, citizens and businesses should, I have said, only be required to give up the right to have their obligations determined by a human judicial decision in favour of machine-made judicial decisions with their eyes open, with their fully informed consent and after the necessary legislative changes have been made following a mature and careful debate.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence and the Judiciary — Sir Geoffrey Vos MR, lecture to the Judicial Institute for Scotland (Edinburgh, 30 April 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: The parties can engage a human arbitrator or arbitrators or, if they wish, they can agree that their disputes will be finally determined by a machine.
qs.a: AI in Arbitration — Promises and Pitfalls — Sir Geoffrey Vos MR, remarks to the BIICL / Jones Day panel, London International Disputes Week (Jones Day offices, London, 4 June 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Unrepresented users cannot simply inherit safeguards designed around expert verification.
kps.d: The consumer-claims article argues that users may neither identify their legal problem nor check generated guidance. England and Wales guidance acknowledges that chatbots may supply some litigants’ only assistance while leaving them responsible for submissions. This creates a deployment disagreement: NYSBA encourages public-facing innovation, whereas testimony in the 2025 access-to-justice report recommends starting with supervised internal court tools. Markovic adds an adversarial qualification: sophisticated actors could use cheaper litigation against poorer people, increasing rather than reducing unmet need. Proposed responses include trained intermediaries, user testing, continued access to advice and protection against digital exclusion.

qs.q: The uses of AI in ODR for small value consumer disputes must necessarily be quite different because the information will be used by non-legally qualified parties who do not have legal representation and may have already made their own inquiries through free, generalist tools such as ChatGPT.
qs.a: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Small Value Consumer Claims: Hallucination Risk, System Design, and Governance in Online Dispute Resolution · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Litigants rarely have the skills independently to verify legal information provided by AI chatbots and may not be aware that they are prone to error.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence (AI): Guidance for Judicial Office Holders (31 October 2025 refresh) · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Verification remains a concrete professional duty, but its feasibility and effectiveness remain contested.
kps.d: Ayinde/Al-Haroun requires lawyers to check AI-assisted research against authoritative sources before reliance, including when others produced the work, and calls for action by professional leaders and regulators. Judicial guidance likewise preserves personal responsibility and direct review of evidence. The Verification-Value Paradox questions confidence that lawyers can reliably manage these risks, drawing on judicial criticism of fabricated filings rather than quantified verification costs. Canadian guidance also flags possible limits to future verification. Vos’s April 2026 claim that earlier hallucination objections have largely been falsified supplies no measurements that resolve these concerns. Litigation incidents establish concrete failures, not model-wide error rates.

qs.q: Those who use artificial intelligence to conduct legal research notwithstanding these            risks have a professional duty therefore to check the accuracy of such research by            reference to authoritative sources, before using it in the course of their professional            work (to advise clients or before a court, for example).
qs.a: R (Ayinde) v London Borough of Haringey; Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank — Divisional Court Judgment on AI Hallucinations and the Hamid Jurisdiction · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: However, the increasing number of cases where judges have criticised lawyers for filing hallucinated AI-generated material with courts calls this paradigm into question.
qs.a: The Verification-Value Paradox: A Normative Critique of Gen AI Use in Legal Practice · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Existing applications and task benchmarks support bounded assistance, not demonstrated autonomous justice.
kps.d: Reported uses include technology-assisted disclosure, SUPACE retrieval, judicial summarisation experiments and administrative search. These involve different technologies and supervision arrangements. Vos’s AAA-ICDR example retains human review of draft awards; his inference about eBay automation does not establish autonomous arbitration. The 2025 symposium address reports Vals AI results favouring legal tools on specified document and transcript tasks, not judicial decision quality. Conversely, the European Ethical Charter reports flawed French prediction experiments at the development stage it assessed. Neither earlier failures nor later task successes establish universal capability, and the supplied judicial survey comments do not quantify adoption or outcomes.

qs.q: It is offering a "human in the loop" model, where the AI arbitrator will evaluate the merits of claims and prepare draft award, but a human arbitrator will review it to test the reasoning and evaluate the decision, in order to quote safeguard trust, transparency and due process.
qs.a: AI in Arbitration — Promises and Pitfalls — Sir Geoffrey Vos MR, remarks to the BIICL / Jones Day panel, London International Disputes Week (Jones Day offices, London, 4 June 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: *All four tools *outperformed the lawyers in the summarisation of documents and the analysis of transcripts, and Harvey Assistant, the platform developed by the eponymous legal technology start-up, even outperformed the lawyers in three additional areas – data extraction, the generation of chronologies, and document review and analysis.
qs.a: The Future of the Legal Profession: A Shared Vision — Opening Address at the Legal Profession Symposium 2025 · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Court governance must address institutional independence and contestability as well as output errors.
kps.d: Canadian guidance warns that proprietary dependence, commercial incentives and purchasing influence could compromise judicial independence. The European Charter identifies a separate risk that statistical trends become unofficial decision standards or tools for monitoring judges. The ABA Year 2 report warns about AI-derived influences parties cannot rebut. Security concerns extend to confidential data, deepfakes and concealed document prompts. Practical recommendations favour judicial involvement in procurement, secure systems, lifecycle impact assessment and locally adapted safeguards. Disclosure remains jurisdiction- and context-dependent: England and Wales does not require routine disclosure of preparatory work, while other reported practices require certifications or disclosure.

qs.q: The planning, procurement, and deployment of generative AI in Canadian courts must firmly uphold the fundamental principle of judicial independence, encompassing its individual and institutional dimensions.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Canadian Courts (Canadian Judicial Council, First Edition, September 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: In these systems, we can- not rule out the risk that such norms will place indirect pressure on judges when decisions are taken and prompt their approval, or that the executive will monitor those who depart from the norm.
qs.a: European Ethical Charter on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Judicial Systems and their Environment · Regulators & courts · 2018

kps.k: Responsible adoption requires institutional reform and sustained human competence, not merely rules or software.
kps.d: COSCA recommends defining the court’s problem before selecting technology and accepts that AI may not help. Canadian guidance proposes pilots, continuing assessment, education and technical support; access-to-justice testimony adds long-term affordability concerns. Bibas and Vos advocate procedural simplification alongside technology, while Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice predicts that political constraints may instead leave judges improvising with imperfect procedural tools. Training presents a further tension: automation may release time for judgment while removing the repetitive work that develops it. Judicial interviews express deskilling fears, not longitudinal findings; educational proposals preserve substantive law, supervision, reflective practice and technological literacy.

qs.q: AI might be helpful or it might not, but what should guide your inquiry into possible technological help should be the needs of your court, not a desire to use one particular piece of software.43  In conclusion, COSCA believes that generative AI is neither the panacea nor the poison that it has been breathlessly proclaimed by the vendors and the pundits.
qs.a: Generative AI and the Future of the Courts: Responsibilities and Possibilities · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Best practices advocate commencing with a pilot project or establishing a controlled testing environment, known as a sandbox, to allow users to assess AI’s capabilities without incurring the risks of a full-scale deployment.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Canadian Courts (Canadian Judicial Council, First Edition, September 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

vlens.an: The supplied market-analysis/press source does not assess the cluster’s principal proposition that technical accuracy cannot itself confer legitimate judicial authority. Instead, it redirects the inquiry from machine adjudication to AI’s effects on the legal profession: unequal access to AI and the erosion of repetitive junior work through which lawyers traditionally develop professional judgement. It intersects with the cluster’s concern about sustaining human competence, but does not address consent, challenge rights, judicial authority, legal development or public confidence. Internal variation is limited in the supplied evidence because this professional voice is represented by a single source; within that source, the emphasis divides between distributive effects across India’s profession and changes to apprenticeship, with neither constituting a position for or against autonomous judging.

qs.q: The consequence is not that lawyers become redundant, but that the profession’s primary mechanism for producing professional judgement is beginning to change.
qs.a: When AI Becomes a Colleague: The Future of India's Legal Profession · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: For India's over one million enrolled advocates, most outside the small tier of AI-equipped commercial firms, the question is no longer whether generative AI will be used but how unevenly its costs and benefits will be distributed.
qs.a: When AI Becomes a Colleague: The Future of India's Legal Profession · Market & press · 2026

vlens.an: Across this curated set of academic and research sources, the principal proposition is broadly accepted and materially developed: predictive accuracy, consistency, speed or low cost do not by themselves confer legitimate judicial authority. Common reasons include the contestable and deliberative nature of legal judgment; the need for human control over lawmaking and social-value choices; identifiable accountability; opportunities to be heard and receive an acceptable justification; and the opacity, embedded values and prompt sensitivity of AI outputs. The sources extend the proposition into practical governance by advocating bounded assistance, human verification, judicial oversight, context-specific safeguards for unrepresented users, and education that preserves ethical judgment. Material internal variation concerns emphasis and scope rather than a shared comprehensive theory. Some sources make philosophical claims about moral judgment or subjective experience; others focus on rule-of-law legitimacy, institutional integrity, access-to-justice inequalities, verification failures or professional training. Several address legal services and lawyer augmentation rather than adjudicative authority, one redirects toward cost- and capability-driven restructuring of legal work, and others leave the central legitimacy question unresolved. A further qualification is comparative: criticism of AI should not idealise human judging, whose reasoning and biases may also be opaque. These selected sources therefore strengthen and broaden the cluster’s proposition without establishing that this position characterises academia or research generally.

Across this curated set, regulators, courts and professional bodies generally accept the proposition that technical accuracy, speed or impartiality cannot by themselves confer legitimate judicial authority. They materially develop it into practical governance requirements: judges retain responsibility and direct engagement; affected parties need awareness, understanding and meaningful opportunities to challenge or appeal; and adoption must protect due process, judicial independence, transparency, professional accountability and public confidence. The principal justification is institutional rather than anti-technology: many sources welcome AI for research, drafting, administration and access to justice while distinguishing those assistive functions from adjudicative delegation. Material variation concerns how firm and enduring that boundary should be. Some guidance categorically prohibits delegation regardless of capability; other sources anticipate machine decisions in routine or consensual disputes but condition them on party choice, informed consent, legislation or human appeal. A smaller strand redirects attention toward court overload and questions whether judging inherently requires a human element, while task-benchmark and workforce-focused sources do not directly address adjudicative legitimacy. These differences concern permitted scope and future pathways, not a shared rejection of AI use in courts.

qs.q: It must be unequivocally understood that no judge is permitted to delegate decision-making authority, whether to a law clerk, administrative assistant, or computer program, regardless of their capabilities.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Canadian Courts (Canadian Judicial Council, First Edition, September 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Liberty and security: Ensure that individuals are not detained based on decisions as-                     sisted by AI that the individual is not aware of, is unable to understand how the AI                     system reached its decision or is unable to challenge or appeal the decision-making                     process or the decision itself.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of AI Systems in Courts and Tribunals · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: The AI-native legal provider source supports the cluster’s principal proposition that technical performance or unchanged outcomes cannot by themselves confer legitimate judicial authority. Its central reason is procedural legitimacy: an almost instantaneous automated decision may leave people feeling that their case was neither heard nor genuinely considered, even where the result matches what a human court would have reached. It also treats AI as only one component of court reform, noting implementation delays and the need for wider system improvements. Internal variation is limited to emphasis rather than direction: the source does not reject court AI, but distinguishes its usefulness from its sufficiency and predicts that trust in rapid machine judgment would take time to develop. These are forecasts and analogies, not empirical evidence about public confidence or adjudicative outcomes. Because this facet contains one curated source, no broader view among AI-native legal providers can be inferred.

qs.q: And if you build a court system that happened in milliseconds I think a lot of people would complain that they don't feel like their case has been heard and listened to even if it was the same outcome.
qs.a: Daniel Long: The Reality Behind Building an AI-Powered Law Firm · AI-native providers · 2026

qs.q: I think everyone wants to see someone deliberating over their situation and giving it some thought.
qs.a: Daniel Long: The Reality Behind Building an AI-Powered Law Firm · AI-native providers · 2026

elens.an: The curated 2015–2022 sources collectively accept and materially develop the proposition that technical accuracy or capability cannot by itself confer legitimate adjudicative authority. They supply several foundations for that distinction: judgment involves contestable interpretation, deliberation and legal-system integrity; accountability must remain attributable; parties must receive an acceptable justification and an opportunity to be heard; and judicial AI must preserve fundamental rights, judicial independence and access to a human judge. They generally favour bounded assistance, calibrated reliance and human supervision rather than binary rejection of AI. Material internal variation concerns why humans should remain involved and how far automation may go. Some sources make institutional and rule-of-law arguments; others offer a conditional philosophical claim that moral judgment may require subjective experience. Lawyer-focused sources distinguish automatable prediction or routine tasks from contextual human judgment, while one redirects attention toward cost, client outcomes and workforce restructuring, and another does not reach adjudicative legitimacy at all. The period’s technical assessments also vary: some report then-current unreliability or limited contextual reasoning, whereas others anticipate more accurate and economical prediction and insist that AI be compared with imperfect human decision-making. Those contingent capability claims do not resolve the more durable legitimacy concerns developed across the period.

Across this curated 2023–2024 selection, the sources generally accept the proposition that technical accuracy, efficiency or apparent impartiality cannot by themselves confer legitimate judicial authority. They materially develop it into a governance programme: retain accountable human decision-makers; distinguish AI-informed from AI-made decisions; preserve due process, contestability, judicial independence and public confidence; and require verification, competence, procurement controls, impact assessment and continuing review. Common reasons are that adjudication includes discretion, fact-sensitive interpretation, ethical judgment and choices about legal development; AI lacks professional duties and institutional accountability; and even accurate outputs may remain opaque, unlawful, biased or inconsistent with court values. Most claimed benefits—access to legal information, lower costs, administrative efficiency and reduced human bias—are prospective rather than demonstrated outcomes, while hallucination cases illustrate concrete misuse rather than model-wide error rates. Material variation concerns how firm the boundary should be. Canadian guidance categorically bars delegation regardless of capability, whereas NYSBA treats AI adjudication as an uncertain future possibility and is more open to consensual AI arbitration or limited small-claims uses. Other sources endorse transparent decision support alongside humans, and COSCA redirects attention toward problem-led institutional adoption without directly resolving autonomous adjudication. Two education-focused or judicial-support sources do not squarely address the legitimacy question, so their positions remain unclear rather than contrary. The Roberts material appears both directly and through an ABA report that republishes it, so it should not be treated as independent corroboration. No source in this period clearly argues that accuracy alone establishes judicial authority, but this curated set should not be read as representative of all judicial, professional or academic views.

qs.q: It must be unequivocally understood that no judge is permitted to delegate decision-making authority, whether to a law clerk, administrative assistant, or computer program, regardless of their capabilities.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Canadian Courts (Canadian Judicial Council, First Edition, September 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Human decision-making and human accountability, expressed through the work of lawyers and advocates, judges and magistrates, and courts and tribunals is the foundation of law.
qs.a: The Future is Now: Artificial Intelligence and the Legal Profession · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an: The curated 2025 sources support the proposition that expanding AI capability and adoption do not themselves confer legitimate judicial authority. Institutional guidance, court judgments and professional materials generally permit bounded assistance while retaining human responsibility, direct engagement with evidence, verification and safeguards for judicial integrity. Rights-oriented sources add procedural fairness, transparency, understanding, challenge and appeal requirements; access-to-justice scholarship further argues that deployment must account for unequal legal knowledge, digital exclusion and adversarial use. Material variation concerns scope and emphasis rather than rejection of the proposition: some sources focus only on legal-practice augmentation or task benchmarks and therefore do not establish a position on autonomous adjudication; others contemplate machine decisions as a potentially attractive future option because of speed and cost, but still treat their authority as a societal, constitutional and institutional question. Several claimed benefits—including faster justice, wider access and sector-wide transformation—remain predictions or inferences from discrete applications and task-level performance, not demonstrated outcomes of autonomous judging.

qs.q: This foundational principle recognizes that judicial authority is vested solely in judicial officers, not in AI systems.
qs.a: Addressing the Legal Challenges of AI: Year 2 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Liberty and security: Ensure that individuals are not detained based on decisions as-                     sisted by AI that the individual is not aware of, is unable to understand how the AI                     system reached its decision or is unable to challenge or appeal the decision-making                     process or the decision itself.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of AI Systems in Courts and Tribunals · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources overall support the proposition that technical accuracy, speed or impartiality cannot by themselves establish legitimate machine authority to judge. The common reasoning is that adjudication also depends on human accountability, direct engagement with the record, verification, constitutional authorization, informed consent, rights protection, legal development and public confidence. Judicial comments and court-policy material therefore generally confine AI to bounded, reviewable assistance, while warnings about hallucinated material illustrate concrete verification failures rather than model-wide error rates. Material variation concerns how far the proposition permits future automation. Vos predicts machine determination of routine disputes but conditions imposed court adjudication on legislation, informed consent and retained human roles, while distinguishing consensual machine arbitration. Other sources stress the experience of being heard, deskilling, unequal access and the possibility that AI-generated filings could increase rather than reduce court workload. Two sources redirect attention toward court-capacity pressures or changes to professional apprenticeship, and one law-firm source does not address adjudicative legitimacy. These differences do not amount to a clear rejection of the proposition. Much of the material consists of forecasts, normative arguments, policy requirements, interviews or anecdotal reports rather than measured evidence of autonomous adjudication’s accuracy, throughput or public acceptance; the curated sources should not be treated as representative of all judges, practitioners or institutions.

qs.q: In a democratic society, citizens and businesses should, I have said, only be required to give up the right to have their obligations determined by a human judicial decision in favour of machine-made judicial decisions with their eyes open, with their fully informed consent and after the necessary legislative changes have been made following a mature and careful debate.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence and the Judiciary — Sir Geoffrey Vos MR, lecture to the Judicial Institute for Scotland (Edinburgh, 30 April 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: And if you build a court system that happened in milliseconds I think a lot of people would complain that they don't feel like their case has been heard and listened to even if it was the same outcome.
